title: 8 Things Teachers Do To Cause Boredom
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin catalogs eight common teacher habits that unintentionally cause student boredom, which he links directly to misbehavior. The list includes keeping students seated too long, talking too much, overcomplicating simple content, failing to make genuinely interesting material feel interesting, talking about behavior instead of acting on it, over-directing while under-observing, running a slow or sloppy pace, and failing to adjust when students visibly disengage. Each item includes a short explanation of the underlying mechanism and a suggested corrective habit. He closes by framing boredom as a fine line just past productive time-on-task, arguing that avoiding these eight mistakes keeps students both engaged and well-behaved.
points: Eight specific teacher habits — including sitting too long, over-talking, and over-complicating content — are identified as direct causes of student boredom.
Overcomplicating simple content in the name of 'rigor' is called out as counterproductive; effective teaching simplifies and cuts non-essentials.
Talking about behavior in class meetings and discussions, rather than taking direct action, is listed among the causes of disengagement.
Over-directing and under-observing — constant micromanaging rather than relying on well-taught routines — is named as a boredom driver.
Failing to adjust when students visibly disengage (heads wilting) is flagged as a mistake worth correcting immediately rather than pushing through.
quotes: For where there is boredom, there is misbehavior percolating just under the surface, ready to pounce.

Many teachers misunderstand the oft-heard mandate for more rigor. They take it to mean that they need to make their instruction more complex, more involved, more verbose—which is a major reason why students don’t progress.

Most standard grade-level subject matter is interesting, but your students don’t know that. In fact, many assume, based on their learning experiences in the past, that it’s boring. It’s your job to show them otherwise.

Teachers who struggle with classroom management tend to talk endlessly about behavior. They hold class meetings. They hash things out. They revisit the same tired topic over and over, much to their students’ eye-rolling chagrin.

And when students cross that line and into boredom, misbehavior is sure to follow. The good news is that by avoiding the common mistakes listed above, you can keep boredom at bay and inspired learning in the spotlight.
